title: Queues, streams and delivery guarantees
summary: Messaging decouples the service that produces work from the services that process it, and the design decisions are which model carries each flow and which guarantees it pays for. This lesson separates a queue from a partitioned log, explains partitions, keys and consumer groups, derives at-most-once and at-least-once from the order of two operations, says exactly what exactly-once covers, treats backlogs as the failure mode they are, sets durability from acknowledgements and in-sync replicas, and turns it into two decision blocks: the neutral model per flow, and the AWS service among SQS standard and FIFO, SNS, EventBridge, Kinesis Data Streams and MSK against ordering, replay, fan-out, throughput, retention and cost, with a worked sizing of an order-event log and its backlog plan.

blocks.text: LinkedIn's Kafka paper describes the deployment the design came from: a cluster in each datacenter receiving batched publishes from the frontends, online consumers in the same datacenter, and a replica cluster next to Hadoop pulling from them, with end-to-end latency of about ten seconds without tuning and close to a billion messages a day at the time. Messages carried an Avro schema id resolved through a lightweight schema registry, and an audit system compared per-producer counts against consumed counts to prove no data was lost.

blocks.caption: Confluent's measured overhead of exactly-once in Kafka 0.11, from the write-up.
rows: transactional producer against at-least-once in-order (acks all, one in flight)
transactional producer against the fastest unordered default
Streams exactly-once at a 100 ms commit interval
15 to 30 percent lower, depending on message size

blocks.text: Slack's job queue ran on Redis until a database slowdown filled Redis to its memory limit; with no free memory it could neither enqueue nor, because dequeuing also needed memory, dequeue, and the system stayed locked after the database recovered. The fix put Kafka in front of Redis: a Go gateway writes jobs to Kafka, waiting only for the leader's acknowledgement by choice, and a relay drains each topic into Redis at a rate set in Consul, taking a Consul lock per topic so exactly one relay owns it. The cluster ran sixteen brokers with thirty-two partitions per topic, a replication factor of three and two days of retention; the rollout double-wrote to both systems and compared counts at every hop.

Amazon's Lambda service does not poll a queue per customer and does not share one queue either: it provisions a fixed set of queues, hashes each customer to a few of them, and enqueues to the emptiest, so a surge backs up only its own queues. AWS IoT measures the age of a message at its first delivery attempt to tell a system-wide backlog from devices reading slowly, and Amazon's teams alarm on any message reaching a dead-letter queue and heartbeat long-running SQS messages so an overloaded consumer does not re-receive its own work.

RabbitMQ's own documentation sets the operating defaults for a classic broker: manual acknowledgement with a prefetch in the hundreds, automatic requeue of unacknowledged deliveries when a channel closes so consumers must expect redelivery, publisher confirms rather than transactions, and a quorum queue's confirm sent only once a quorum of replicas holds the message.

subtopics.title: A queue and a log are different things

blocks.text: Messaging decouples the service that produces work from the services that process it, in time and in capacity. Two designs do that decoupling, and they behave differently under failure, under backlog and when a new reader arrives. A message queue hands each message to one worker, waits for an acknowledgement, and then forgets the message. A log appends every message to a durable ordered file, keeps it for a retention period whether or not anyone has read it, and lets each reader keep its own position.

The Kafka paper states the second design's consequences in one page. A message has no id, only its offset in the partition; the broker keeps no record of what a consumer has read, so the consumer tracks its own offset and acknowledges by position; messages are deleted by a time-based retention policy, typically a week; and because of that a consumer can deliberately rewind to an old offset and read again, which the authors note violates the usual contract of a queue but turned out to be essential, for fixing a consumer bug or reloading a warehouse. The current design document adds why the position is cheap: one integer per partition instead of per-message state on the broker.

blocks.text: The queue model is what a task system needs: jobs, emails, image resizes, where each item is independent, must be retried on its own and should disappear when done. The log model is what an event backbone needs: facts that several systems will read, in order per entity, with the right to be replayed. The Kafka design document puts the throughput case for the log, appends and linear reads on cheap disks with the page cache doing the caching, and the paper puts the semantic case, the rewind.

Ask what the payload is before picking the transport. A command for one worker belongs on a queue; an event that is a fact many systems will consume belongs on a log. A log can imitate a queue through consumer groups, but per-message retry and delay are where the imitation strains.

A log scales by partitioning a topic. Each partition is an ordered append-only sequence stored on a broker and replicated; the producer chooses the partition, at random for load balancing or by hashing a key, so that every record with the same key lands in the same partition and stays in order. That makes the key the first design decision of a topic: the entity whose events must be ordered, an order id or an account id, not a timestamp and not a random value. Order holds within a partition only, never across the topic.

blocks.legend: One topic, three partitions, two consumer groups. Within a group each partition has exactly one reader; each group reads the whole topic independently. A record that keeps failing is moved to a dead-letter topic so the partition can advance.

blocks.text: Consumers that share a group id divide the partitions among themselves. The paper's two decisions still stand: a partition is the unit of parallelism, read by one consumer per group at a time so that no locking is needed between readers; and a topic should have many more partitions than consumers so that load balances, which the authors call over-partitioning. Different groups read the same topic independently with their own offsets and need no coordination with each other. When a member joins or dies the group rebalances and partitions are reassigned; the new owner resumes from the last committed offset, which is the moment duplicates appear.

blocks.text: Two newer mechanisms soften the sharp edges. Static membership gives a consumer a persistent instance id so that a restart or deploy does not trigger a rebalance and a reshuffle of partitions, which matters for consumers with large local state. Share groups, a second kind of group in the current design, let more consumers than partitions read cooperatively with per-record acknowledgement, a time-limited acquisition lock of thirty seconds by default, and counted delivery attempts, which is the queue model offered on top of the log.

Pick the key for ordering and the partition count for the parallelism you will need in a year, because changing the count later remaps keys. A hot key, one account producing most of the traffic, defeats both: it serialises on one partition whatever the count.

subtopics.title: At-most-once, at-least-once and the order of two operations

blocks.text: The delivery guarantee is not a property of the broker alone; it comes from the order in which a consumer does two things, process the message and record that it has done so. The Kafka design document lays out both orders. Save the position first, then process: a crash between the two loses the messages whose position was saved, which is at-most-once. Process first, then save the position: a crash between the two makes the new owner process those messages again, which is at-least-once. The producer side has the same fork: a producer that retries after a timeout may write the same message twice unless the broker can detect it.

blocks.caption: The three guarantees and where each comes from.
rows: make processing idempotent: duplicates will arrive
keep side effects inside the transaction's reach, or make them idempotent too

blocks.text: Every broker expresses the same choice in its own vocabulary. RabbitMQ's documentation calls automatic acknowledgement, where a message counts as delivered the moment it is written to the socket, unsafe and unsuitable for most workloads, because a closed connection loses it; manual acknowledgement with a bounded prefetch, usually in the range of a hundred to a few hundred, is the normal mode, and any unacknowledged delivery is requeued when the channel closes, so consumers must be written for redelivery. A rejected message is requeued, dead-lettered or discarded, and a loop of requeues on a transient error is a known cost to guard against.

SQS expresses it as a visibility timeout: a received message stays in the queue but is hidden from other consumers for a period, thirty seconds by default, extendable with a heartbeat up to a maximum of twelve hours; delete it before the timeout and it is gone, fail to and it reappears for another consumer. The guide is explicit that the model is at-least-once and that a message may be delivered more than once even inside the timeout. The practical default across all three is therefore the same: at-least-once delivery with an idempotent consumer, because a lost message is usually worse than a duplicate.

Write every consumer for duplicates: record the message id or use an upsert, commit the position after the side effect, and bound the retries. The broker's acknowledgement mode decides which failure you get; the consumer's idempotency decides whether it matters.

Exactly-once is the guarantee everyone wants and the one most often claimed loosely. The Kafka design document warns that many such claims do not survive the fine print: consumer failures, several consumer processes, or lost disk writes. What Kafka itself provides since version 0.11 rests on two mechanisms. The idempotent producer attaches a producer id and a sequence number to every batch, persisted in the replicated log, so a retried batch is discarded by the broker rather than written twice, within one partition and in order. Transactions let a producer write to several partitions atomically and commit the consumer's position in the same transaction, so that a read-process-write loop that stays inside Kafka takes effect once.

blocks.caption: What Kafka's exactly-once covers, from the design document and the Confluent write-up.

a transaction: all visible or none
read from Kafka, process, write to Kafka
offsets committed inside the same transaction; consumers read with read_committed
a database write or an API call made by the consumer

a consumer that rewinds on purpose
it will receive everything again; the application and the broker must cooperate

blocks.text: The cost is small by the authors' measurement: with a transaction every hundred milliseconds, producer throughput fell by about three percent against an at-least-once producer and by about twenty percent against the fastest, unordered setting, and the idempotent producer alone had negligible overhead. The price that remains is latency, because a read-committed consumer sees a transaction's records only when it commits, so the commit interval sets the end-to-end delay.

Outside the broker the word changes meaning, and a queue's promise ends at the queue. SQS FIFO queues order messages strictly within a message group, and the AWS decision guide describes SQS delivery as at-least-once with the possibility of duplicates; neither statement says anything about what the consumer does with a message. The design document's own general advice is the one that applies everywhere: let the consumer store its offset in the same place as its output, so that the two are updated together or not at all, as a connector writing files with their offsets does.

Exactly-once is a property of a closed loop. The moment the consumer touches a system outside it, the guarantee is whatever that system's write gives you, and the only portable answer is an idempotent write keyed by the message.

subtopics.title: Backlogs, lag, backpressure and dead letters

blocks.text: A queue does not remove overload; it moves it in time. Amazon's Builders' Library describes the result as bimodal behaviour: with no backlog, latency is low and the system is in its fast mode; once arrivals exceed the processing rate it flips into a mode where end-to-end latency grows and recovery takes a long time, so the queue that was added for availability now causes the availability loss it was meant to prevent. The arithmetic is unforgiving: an hour's outage needs double the capacity for an hour afterwards, and a backlog ten times the consumer capacity, built in the half hour before anyone notices, takes five hours to drain.

The metric that catches it is the age of messages, not the error rate. The producer's success rate mirrors the queue service's availability and the consumer's error rate is polluted by retries that then succeed; the age of the oldest message, or the age at first delivery attempt as AWS IoT measures it to filter out slow readers, shows how far behind the system is. On a log the equivalent is consumer lag, the gap between the latest offset and the committed one, and retention must be set so that lag cannot outrun it.

blocks.caption: Amazon's techniques for a backlog that will not drain, from the Builders' Library.

move a noisy tenant's messages, or messages past an age, to a spillover queue worked after the live one
throttle the producer in proportion to the backlog of its workload
re-enqueue work to be hidden for minutes, giving fresh messages priority
where a periodic full sync will correct the state anyway
keep spare polling capacity so a spike does not become sustained backlog

blocks.text: Poison messages need their own exit. A message that fails every time blocks a partition or cycles for ever through a queue; the answer is a bounded number of retries with backoff and then a dead-letter queue or topic, alarmed on, with a way to replay after the fix. SQS attaches that policy to the queue and recommends it for persistent failures; RabbitMQ routes a rejected delivery to a dead-letter exchange when one is configured; Amazon's teams alarm on any message in a dead-letter queue because it means a bug.

Alert on message age, not on queue depth or error rate. Decide before launch what the system does when the backlog exceeds an hour of capacity: shed at the producer, sideline, or drop, because draining in order is the one answer that never recovers on time.

subtopics.title: What durable means: acknowledgements, in-sync replicas and confirms

blocks.text: A message is durable when the broker will not lose it after acknowledging it, and the acknowledgement is a dial. In Kafka a message is committed only when every replica in the in-sync set has applied it; the producer chooses whether to wait for that, with acks set to all, to wait for the leader only, or not to wait at all. Two topic settings turn durability up further: a minimum in-sync replica count, so that a write cannot succeed on a lone surviving replica, and disabling unclean leader election, so that a partition stays unavailable rather than elect a replica that may lack committed messages.

blocks.caption: The producer's acknowledgement setting in Kafka and what it buys.
rows: no failure; a lost send is never known
a follower failure; a leader crash before replication loses the message
every in-sync replica, at least the minimum configured
any failure that leaves one in-sync replica alive

blocks.text: Kafka's in-sync-replica design is a deliberate departure from majority quorums: with f plus one replicas it tolerates f failures, where a majority scheme needs two f plus one, at the price of waiting for every in-sync replica rather than the fastest majority. The document argues the saving in disk and throughput is worth it for bulk data, and that a replica that crashed and lost unflushed data must fully resynchronise before it rejoins the in-sync set.

Traditional brokers expose the same dial under other names. RabbitMQ's publisher confirms are the only cheap way to know a publish was not lost; transactions do the same at a two-hundred-and-fifty-fold throughput cost. A confirm for a persistent message to a durable queue is sent after the message is written to disk, batched every few hundred milliseconds, or for a quorum queue once a quorum of replicas has it, and the documentation shows the trap of consuming without confirms: a broker restart loses a message the publisher believed was persistent.

Set durability per topic from what losing a message costs: acks all with a minimum of two in-sync replicas and no unclean election for money and orders; leader-only acknowledgement for logs and metrics where a rare loss is cheaper than the latency.

subtopics.title: Choosing: queue, log, topic or bus

blocks.text: The choice is per flow, not per organisation, and it starts with the payload: a command for one worker, an event for many readers, a notification for people, or a stream to be analysed. The decision below is vendor-neutral; the next subtopic maps each option to the AWS services the exercises use. The example column names the flow each option is usually right for.

blocks.caption: Picking the messaging model for one flow.

rows.pick_when: each message is an independent job for exactly one worker, must be retried and delayed on its own, and can be forgotten once done
rows.avoid_when: several systems need the same event, or a reader must be able to replay history
rows.example: sending emails; resizing images; running a billing job

rows.pick_when: jobs for one entity must run in order, at a lower throughput per group
rows.avoid_when: the per-group ceiling is below the entity's event rate
rows.example: the operations on one order; one customer's commands

rows.pick_when: events are facts that several consumers read at their own pace, order per key matters, replay and backfill are valuable, throughput is high
rows.avoid_when: work items need individual retry and delay, or ordering is not needed and a queue is simpler to operate
rows.example: order events feeding billing, search, analytics and fraud

rows.pick_when: one message must reach several subscribers now, each with its own queue or function, including push to people
rows.avoid_when: subscribers need to read the past; the topic does not persist
rows.example: an order placed event fanned out to fulfilment, a warehouse and a test environment

rows.pick_when: many sources route to many targets by content, across accounts or SaaS, with transformation on the way
rows.avoid_when: strict ordering or very high throughput per route is required
rows.example: integration events between teams and third-party tools

blocks.text: Two combinations recur. A topic or bus in front of a queue gives fan-out plus a durable buffer per consumer, which is how the AWS application-integration guide describes sending events to a queue as a buffer for downstream consumers. A log behind a thin gateway gives a durable, replayable buffer in front of an older system, which is what Slack built when its Redis-backed job queue ran out of memory: Kafka absorbs the enqueue rate and a relay drains it into Redis at a configured rate.

Start from the consumer: one worker that must retry, a queue; many readers that may replay, a log; many targets to notify now, a topic; many sources to route, a bus. Then size the partition or group count from the ordering key and the year's throughput.

blocks.text: AWS offers the five models as six services: SQS pulls, SNS pushes, EventBridge routes by rule, Kinesis and MSK are logs. Its messaging guide compares the first three on persistence, delivery, ordering and filtering; its application-integration guide separates messaging from streaming and names replay and ordering as the deciding criteria. worked_example.title: Worked example: an order-event log at 20,000 events per second, and its backlog plan

blocks.text: An e-commerce platform publishes every order change as an event that billing, search, analytics and fraud each consume. The team must size the log, pick the key, set durability, and decide in advance what happens when a consumer falls an hour behind. Every input is an assumption chosen to make the arithmetic concrete; the mechanics are the Kafka design document's and the backlog rules are the Builders' Library's.

blocks.title: From the event rate to partitions, replicas, retention and a drain plan
items: Events: 5,000 order events per second on average, 20,000 at peak (assumption), of about 1 kB each.
Peak write bandwidth: 20,000 events of 1 kB is 20 MB/s into the log, before replication.
Ordering key: the order id, so every change to one order lands in one partition in sequence.
Consumer capacity: one billing consumer handles 2,000 events per second including its database write (assumption from a load test), so the peak needs 10 consumers in the billing group.
Partition count: at least 10 for the consumers, over-partitioned to 30 so the group can triple before the count must change and keys move.
Durability: replication factor 3 with acks set to all and a minimum of 2 in-sync replicas, so a committed order event survives the loss of one broker and a write cannot land on a lone replica.
Retention: 7 days at 5,000 events per second of 1 kB is about 430 GB a day, 3 TB for the week, 9 TB on disk with three replicas.
Backlog: a one-hour billing outage leaves 18 million events (5,000 per second times 3,600); the Builders' Library arithmetic says draining it in an hour needs double the capacity, 20 consumers.
The real limit: 20 consumers would push 40,000 writes per second into the billing database, so the drain is capped at what that database sustains and the recovery time is set by it, not by the log.
Lag alert: a consumer group whose committed offset is more than 5 minutes behind the latest, about 1.5 million events, pages before the backlog becomes insurmountable.
Poison events: an event that fails 3 times with backoff is written to a dead-letter topic with the error attached and the partition moves on; the topic is alarmed and replayed after the fix.

The decider: the billing database's write rate. The log absorbs any burst at 20 MB/s; the time to recover from a consumer outage is the backlog divided by what the slowest dependency can take, so that number goes in the runbook.

# at-least-once consumer with an idempotent handler: process, then commit the position
for msg in consumer:                        # auto commit disabled
    event_id = msg.headers["event-id"]
    with db.transaction() as tx:
        if tx.seen(event_id):               # duplicate after a rebalance or a retry
            consumer.commit(msg)
            continue
        apply_billing_change(tx, msg.value)
        tx.mark_seen(event_id)              # the id lands in the same transaction as the side effect
    consumer.commit(msg)                    # only after the database commit
